name: priority-queue
intent: Keep a collection ordered so the highest-priority element is always available in constant time and each insertion or removal costs logarithmic time, instead of sorting the whole collection or scanning it for the next element.
problem: Work must be processed in priority order - earliest deadline first, shortest job first, highest-value first, Dijkstra's next frontier, the next scheduled event - and the collection of candidates is both large and changing. Sorting on every change is O(n log n) per change, scanning for the minimum is O(n) per step and O(n^2) overall, and keeping a sorted array pays an O(n) insert because every element after the insertion point shifts. A FIFO is wrong because it ignores priority entirely, and a bucket structure only works when the priorities are a small dense range.
context: Applies whenever elements compete for a shared resource and the order of service matters: task schedulers with priority or deadline, Dijkstra and Prim's graph algorithms, event simulation where the next scheduled event is the one to process, Dijkstra-style frontier traversal, top-K selection over a stream where only the K largest or smallest are needed, running-median maintenance with two heaps, k-way merging of sorted streams, bandwidth management, and anytime/best-first search in planning. The choice between heap flavours (binary, d-ary, pairing, radix) and between eager removal and lazy deletion is driven by the priority distribution and the insert/delete ratio, not by aesthetics.
benefits: O(1) access to the extremal element and O(log n) insert and remove, which turns an O(n^2) scan-based scheduler into one that keeps up with its input.
No repeated sorting: the structure maintains the order incrementally, so a priority that changes every iteration costs nothing extra to reorder.
The frontier discipline generalises: Dijkstra, Prim, best-first search, A*, and event simulation are all 'repeatedly take the best available next thing', which is exactly this interface.
Bounded memory with lazy deletion: an entry can be invalidated in O(1) by pushing a replacement and skipping the stale entry when it surfaces, which avoids an O(n) search-and-remove.

d-ary heaps trade one operation for another: a 4-ary heap does far fewer comparisons on sift-down at the cost of shallower memory locality, and that trade is worth several percent on cache-bound workloads.

Tie-breaking is a design decision the structure makes visible: a monotonic counter as a secondary key makes equal priorities come out in insertion order, which is usually the fairness property you actually want.
tradeoffs: No random access and no ordering guarantee beyond the root: iterating a heap yields the internal array order, not sorted order, so 'sort everything' still needs a separate pass (though heappop n times is O(n log n)).

O(n) for decrease-key and removal of an arbitrary element without an auxiliary index. Dijkstra with decrease-key needs a key-to-position map maintained in parallel, or a lazy-deletion variant that accepts stale entries and pushes replacements.

Comparison cost dominates when the comparison is expensive (a comparator that does I/O or a deep structural comparison) - the O(log n) comparisons are then the whole cost, and a partial-sort or bucket approach can beat it.

Priority distribution matters and is often pathological: uniform random keys in a binary heap still sift almost to the bottom on insert, so real-time systems historically used radix or calendar queues, and buckets beat a heap when the key range is small and dense.

Cache behaviour is not great: a binary heap's sift-down walks a tree, so it takes unpredictable branches across cache lines, and even the heapified array form can be slower than the theoretically optimal layout on large heaps.

Ties need a deliberate rule: equal-priority entries compare as equal, so a tuple comparator falls through to comparing the payloads - often raising TypeError or producing arbitrary order - unless a counter is added.
Starvation of low-priority elements is a policy question, not a data-structure one: a priority queue gives the highest priority first forever, and fairness requires ageing or a secondary criterion.

A queue alone does not imply thread-safety: the concurrent variants (PriorityBlockingQueue, channels with priority) reintroduce locking, and the non-blocking ones reintroduce the cpu-atomic-operation record's whole difficulty.
quality_attributes_note: Performance and scalability are the reason for the structure: O(log n) versus O(n) per step is the difference between a scheduler that keeps up and one that does not. Type safety is mid because the comparison contract is easy to violate silently - a comparator that raises on equal keys, or an inconsistent ordering that makes the sift logic produce wrong results rather than an error.

participants.responsibility: Stores the elements as a flat array where children of i live at 2i+1 and 2i+2 and the parent is (i-1)/2, so the tree shape and the storage are the same thing with no pointer chasing.
participants.notes: The array layout is what makes the cache behaviour reasonable and the heap trivially copyable.

participants.responsibility: Every parent dominates (or is dominated by, in a max-heap) both children; the root is therefore always the extremal element.
participants.notes: Maintaining this under insert and remove is the entire algorithm.

participants.responsibility: After an insert, moves the new element up while it outranks its parent, restoring the invariant.
participants.notes: Hole-punching rather than swapping halves the writes per level for non-trivial types.

participants.responsibility: After removing the root, moves the replacement element down, always promoting the smaller (or larger) child so the invariant is not violated on the sibling side.
participants.notes: Promoting the wrong child is the classic hand-rolled-heap bug: the surface looks plausible and corruption appears several pops later.

participants.responsibility: Builds a heap from an unsorted array in linear time by sift-down from the last internal node to the root.
participants.notes: The classic proof that the total cost is O(n), because most nodes are near the leaves.

participants.responsibility: Supplies the total order; must be a consistent strict weak ordering or the sift logic produces garbage.
participants.notes: The most common source of production bugs, especially with ties.

participants.responsibility: A monotonic sequence number that makes entries totally ordered so equal priorities still come out FIFO.
participants.notes: Present in Python's own heapq documentation as the standard solution.

participants.responsibility: A side table from key to heap position, updated on every swap, turning decrease-key and removal-by-key from O(n) into O(log n).
participants.notes: Required by Dijkstra; the reason Sedgewick's IndexMinPQ exists.

use_cases: Task and job schedulers with priorities or deadlines: the next task to run is the heap root, extracted in O(log n) rather than found by scanning.
Dijkstra and Prim's shortest-path algorithms: the frontier is a priority queue, and the index-map variant gives decrease-key instead of pushing duplicates.
Event-driven simulation and discrete-event models: the next scheduled event is by definition the minimum timestamp, which is a min-heap - this is the textbook origin of the structure.
Top-K selection over an unbounded stream, maintaining a heap of size K so memory is O(K) and the cost per element is O(log K) rather than O(log n) or a full sort.
Running-median maintenance with two heaps (max-heap below the median, min-heap above), which the heapq documentation implements in a few lines and which every streaming quantile sketch relies on.
K-way merge of sorted inputs: heapq.merge or a hand-written heap yields the globally smallest remaining element across all sources in O(log K) per step.
Best-first search and A* in planning and scheduling: 'expand the most promising node' is a heap pop, and the frontier can grow unbounded so the heap is the memory bound.
Bandwidth and rate management: send the highest-priority packet first, dropping the rest when the buffer is full.
Bandits and regret minimisation: pull the arm with the highest current estimate of reward, which is a max-heap over arm values.
avoid_when: The collection is small and nearly static - sorting once is O(n log n) total and simpler than maintaining a heap, and a linear scan beats a heap for n under about fifty where cache effects dominate.
You need sorted order over the whole collection, not just the extremum - a heap gives you the root cheaply and the rest unordered, so a sort (or the heap-drain) is still required.
Priority keys are a small dense integer range - a bucket or array of per-priority queues gives O(1) per operation, which beats O(log n) and is what real-time schedulers used before heaps.
Keys are timestamps with a bounded horizon - a calendar queue keyed by time bucket is O(1) amortised and avoids the heap's cache-unfriendly sift.

The comparison is expensive or the comparator is inconsistent - a heap's correctness depends on a strict weak ordering, and a comparator that is merely 'roughly right' produces silently wrong results.
You need decrease-key, removal-by-key, or a keys view - the base structure offers none of these; either add the index map or use lazy deletion and accept stale entries.
The work is actually not competing for anything: if every element must be processed and the order is irrelevant, a FIFO is faster and fairer.
Fairness is required and priorities do not encode urgency - a strict priority queue starves low-priority work indefinitely; add ageing or a secondary arrival key.
pitfalls: Ties: equal-priority entries compare equal, and a tuple comparator then falls through to comparing the payloads, which raises TypeError for incomparable payloads or produces arbitrary order - add a monotonic counter as the second element.

Sift-down promoting the larger child in a min-heap: the heap still looks plausible and corruption surfaces several pops later, which is why differential testing against a reference heap is worth the setup.
Unsigned index arithmetic at the root: parent(0) computed as (0-1)/2 on an unsigned type underflows to an enormous index rather than -1; guard i > 0 before computing the parent.
Reading the right child without first bounds-checking it: the last internal node often has only a left child, so the r < n test must short-circuit first.

heapreplace versus heappushpop: replace always returns an element (possibly larger than the one pushed), pushpop always keeps the smaller of the two - choosing wrongly silently changes the semantics of a streaming algorithm.
Claiming decrease-key exists: std::priority_queue, java.util.PriorityQueue and heapq have no update operation, and reaching for heap[i] and re-sorting breaks the invariant.
A comparator that is not a strict weak ordering (non-transitive, or throwing) makes sift-up and sift-down disagree about what the root is; the failure is silent.

Assuming the concurrent variants are lock-free: PriorityBlockingQueue and a concurrent priority queue reintroduce exactly the locking and contention that made you reach for a priority queue in the first place.

related_patterns_notes.event-queue: The FIFO form of the same structure. An event-queue answers 'what arrives next'; a priority queue answers 'what is most urgent next'. When the queue needs both (a deadline order that must be rescheduled when a task's deadline slips), the priority queue with lazy deletion is the extension.
related_patterns_notes.careful-buffering: Boundedness is the shared decision. A priority queue without a bound is an unbounded buffer whose failure mode is memory exhaustion; an explicit bound with a stated policy - drop lowest, drop highest, reject the newest - is what this catalog's careful-buffering pattern requires, and 'drop lowest' is the policy that makes sense for a priority queue.
related_patterns_notes.producer-consumer: The queue's role in a pipeline is the same, but the priority order changes what the consumer does with the head: a scheduler takes the most urgent item, a pipeline takes the next.
related_patterns_notes.circular-buffer: The storage cousin. A circular buffer gives O(1) FIFO access with no ordering by priority; a heap gives O(log n) access to the extremum. A bounded heap can use an array plus an index map, and a fixed-size ring is the right structure when priority degenerates to arrival order.
related_patterns_notes.iterator: Traversal is the sharpest difference: iterating a heap yields the internal array order, not sorted order, and every standard library documents this. Anyone needing sorted output must sort explicitly or drain the heap.
related_patterns_notes.lock-free-queue: Both are concurrent hand-off structures, and the lock-free one exists to remove contention - which is the same motivation for a concurrent priority queue, but those reintroduce locking because the ordering is the harder part to make non-blocking.
related_patterns_notes.fold-catamorphism: Draining a heap by repeated heappop is a fold over the structure with the comparison as the algebra; the difference is that the heap's interior order is not meaningful, so the fold is the only way to see the data.
related_patterns_notes.monoid: Aggregation over a heap is a fold, and when the aggregate must support parallel combination the combining operation needs to be a monoid - a different requirement from the ordering the heap provides.
related_patterns_notes.encapsulate-collection: The heap is the proof that representation choice is a design decision. A priority queue exposes an ordering interface (peek / enqueue / dequeue) and hides the flat-array-plus-sift implementation, so the algorithm that consumes it (Dijkstra, a scheduler) is written against the interface and never against the storage.
related_patterns_notes.typed-collection: Type parameters carry the element and, where the library separates them, the priority type. That separation is what makes a heterogeneous queue (many payload types, one shared priority) expressible without boxing, and it makes the comparator's contract explicit at the type boundary.

anti_patterns: Sorting the whole collection on every priority change, which is O(n log n) per change when a single sift would do.
A linear scan for the minimum on every step, giving O(n^2) over a run where O(n log n) is available.
Sorting once and inserting into the middle of a sorted array, paying O(n) per insert and assuming the array is cheap to maintain.
Comparing payloads when priorities tie, producing TypeError or arbitrary order instead of FIFO among equals.
Reaching into the underlying container and reordering it by hand, which silently breaks the heap invariant that everything else depends on.
Declaring decrease-key on a library that has none, and hacking it by mutating the internal array - the invariant is gone and the failure is intermittent.
Using a strict priority queue for fair work distribution, so low-priority work is starved forever - add a monotonic arrival counter or an ageing rule.
An unbounded priority queue, which converts a priority inversion problem into an out-of-memory problem; bound it and state the drop policy.
A concurrent priority queue under contention, which reintroduces the lock the structure was chosen to avoid - measure before assuming the priority ordering is worth it.
design_principles: Maintain the extremum, not the order: the structure promises the root is the minimum or maximum, and pays O(log n) to keep that promise rather than keeping the whole collection sorted.
Exploit completeness: storing the tree as a flat array removes pointer chasing and makes the shape free, which is what makes the heap cache-friendly enough to beat scanning.
Make ties explicit: a stable ordering is a decision (FIFO among equals), and it belongs in the key rather than in the comparator's fallback.
Choose the arity and the build from the workload: d-ary for cache-bound sift-down, Floyd's O(n) build for bulk construction, lazy deletion for high invalidation rates.
Bound it: a priority queue in a system with a steady arrival rate is a buffer, and every buffer needs a stated policy at capacity.
best_practices: Add a monotonic counter as the secondary key (heapq's documented approach) so equal priorities come out in insertion order and the payload is never compared.
Use heapreplace or heappushpop rather than heappop followed by heappush on streaming hot paths - it is a single sift-down and roughly twice as fast.
Build with Floyd's linear-time heapify rather than pushing n elements one at a time, which is O(n log n).
Use a d-ary heap (4-ary is the usual choice) when profiling shows comparison-bound sift-down, and keep the binary heap when memory locality dominates.
For decrease-key, maintain a key-to-position index map and update it on every swap, or accept lazy deletion and skip stale entries when they surface.
Reserve capacity up front so push does not reallocate the array in the middle of a latency-sensitive run.

Test with a heapify invariant checker after every mutation in tests (one linear scan comparing each child to its parent), and differential-test against the standard library heap with random operations - a corrupted heap still returns plausible values for several pops.
State the policy at capacity explicitly (drop lowest, drop highest, reject newest, or block) and implement it; an unbounded priority queue is a memory leak with extra steps.
For a running median, keep a max-heap below and a min-heap above and rebalance from the tops - the standard two-heap construction, which heapq documents in a few lines.
In real-time systems with bounded timestamp horizons, prefer a calendar queue over a heap: O(1) amortised per operation and no cache-unfriendly sift.
sources: J. W. J. Williams, 'Algorithm 232 Heapsort' (Communications of the ACM, June 1964) - the original binary heap, packaged inside a sorting routine; Floyd's December 1964 Treesort added the linear bottom-up construction. https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/366030.366400

The DSA Handbook, 'Heaps and priority queues' - the sift-up/sift-down analysis, Floyd's Theta(n) build versus Williams's O(n log n), the operation table with replace as a single sift-down, the defaults that differ across stdlib (Python heapq and Java PriorityQueue are min-heaps, C++ std::priority_queue is a max-heap), and the indexed priority queue Dijkstra needs. https://dsa.handbook.academy/curriculum/trees-heaps/heaps-priority-queues/

Neel Mishra, 'Sift-Up, Sift-Down & Why They Are Correct' - the three hand-rolled-heap bugs that account for most broken implementations (wrong child promoted, unsigned underflow at the root, unchecked right child), and the differential-testing technique against std::priority_queue that catches them. https://neelmishra.github.io/blog/dsa/heap/sift-operations.html

Python documentation, 'heapq - Heap queue algorithm' - the min-heap invariant, heapify/heappush/heappop/heapreplace/heappushpop, merge/nlargest/nsmallest, the tie-breaking counter recipe, the lazy-deletion recipe for remove and priority update, the running-median construction, and the disk-sorting argument for external merge. https://docs.python.org/3/library/heapq.html
